back: The pipe stands upright with its axis vertical, and the weld runs around it horizontally. The pipe is not turned during welding.

front: What is the 5G position on pipe?
back: The pipe is fixed horizontal and cannot be turned. The welder works around it through the flat, vertical, and overhead areas.

front: What is the 6G position on pipe?
back: The pipe is fixed at an angle of 45° to the horizontal and is not turned. It is a hard test because the welder must weld in all areas on one fixed joint.

front: Does qualifying in a harder position cover easier ones?
back: Often it does, but the exact rule depends on the code and the joint type. Generally a pass in the vertical and overhead plate positions covers all plate positions. Always read the code tables rather than assuming.

front: What is the order of precedence in contract documents?
back: It is the list in the contract that says which document wins when two documents disagree. Arrangements differ between contracts. Read the clause in your own contract and never guess.

front: What should be done if two contract documents conflict?
back: Ask the responsible person, often through a written request for information, and wait for a written answer. Do not guess which document to follow. Guessing is how costly mistakes happen.

front: Which documents are usually part of the contract set for a welding job?
back: They usually include the contract itself, the drawings, the project specifications, the referenced codes and standards, and changes such as addenda and change orders.

front: What are the main duties of a welder under the rules?
back: The welder follows the WPS that applies, uses the correct materials and equipment, and welds only within the limits of the qualification held. The welder also cleans between passes, reports problems, and follows safety rules.

front: What are the main duties of a welding inspector?
back: The inspector checks the documents, materials, welder qualifications, and the procedure in use. The inspector examines the work before, during, and after welding and reports whether it meets the code. The inspector does not weld the joint.

front: Who carries the overall duty to make welds meet the contract?
back: The contractor or fabricator who employs the welder carries it. This includes qualifying procedures and welders, controlling the work, and repairing rejected welds. The owner may verify that the work meets the requirements.

front: What does SENSE stand for?
back: SENSE stands for Schools Excelling through National Skills Education. It is an American Welding Society program that sets a national standard for welding education and training. This book prepares students for Level 1 and Level 2.

front: What are QC10 and QC11 in the SENSE program?
back: They are numbers of AWS documents that support the entry level and advanced level qualification and certification work in the program. Know them as labels. Your instructor will say exactly which one applies to which level.

front: What does the SENSE Assessment Coordinator do?
back: The Assessment Coordinator is a person at the school recognized by the program to manage testing. The coordinator makes sure exams and performance tests are given under the proper rules, records are kept, and results are reported correctly.

front: What score is needed to pass a SENSE module knowledge exam?
back: A student needs at least 75 percent. On a 40 question exam, that is 0.75 × 40 = 30 correct answers. A lower score means the module exam is not passed.

front: What score is needed on the SENSE safety exam, and why?
back: The safety exam requires 100 percent. A single safety mistake can injure or kill someone, so the program does not accept a safety score with wrong answers. A student who misses any question must study again and retake it.

front: What is a prequalified WPS?
back: It is a WPS that meets the strict limits set out in the prequalified section of AWS D1.1, so no procedure test is needed. If any part falls outside those limits, the procedure must be qualified by testing and a PQR.

front: What does the G in 1G, 2G, 3G and 4G stand for?
back: G stands for groove weld. F would stand for fillet. The number is the welding position.

front: Describe the 2G plate position.
back: The plate stands upright and the weld runs sideways across it. This is the horizontal position.

front: Describe the 3G plate position.
back: The plate stands upright and the weld runs up or down. This is the vertical position.

front: Describe the 4G plate position.
back: The plate is above the welder and the weld is made from underneath. This is the overhead position.

front: What is a groove angle (included angle)?
back: It is the total angle between the two prepared edges of the joint. Two 30° bevels give a 60° groove angle.

front: What is a root opening?
back: It is the gap between the two pieces at the bottom of the joint. Its size comes from the WPS and is usually wider with backing than for open root.

front: What is a root face (land)?
back: It is the small flat, unbeveled strip at the bottom of a prepared edge. It helps control penetration and burn through.

front: What is the purpose of backing on a groove weld?
back: Backing is a bar tacked behind the joint to support the molten puddle. It makes burn through less likely and is easier to learn than open root.

front: What is an open root joint?
back: An open root joint has no backing behind it. The welder must fuse both edges and form the back bead with nothing to support the puddle.

front: What does a test done with backing qualify for open root joints?
back: A test done with backing does not qualify a welder for open root joints. A test done open root generally qualifies for backed joints, but confirm this in the code.

front: What is a root pass?
back: It is the first pass in the joint. It fuses the root and sets the shape of the back side, and later passes cannot repair a bad one.

front: What is the job of the hot pass?
back: The hot pass is run soon after the root pass at slightly higher current. It burns out slag traps and smooths the root bead edges for the next passes.

front: What are fill passes and the cap pass?
back: Fill passes build the joint up to nearly flush with the plate surface. The cap pass is the last layer and sets the final weld width and reinforcement.

front: What is reinforcement on a groove weld?
back: Reinforcement is extra weld metal standing above the plate surface. Codes limit it, a common limit being about 1/8 inch, but check the code or WPS.

front: What is a keyhole in open root welding?
back: A keyhole is a small round opening at the leading edge of the puddle where the arc has melted through the root face. A steady keyhole shows full penetration.

front: What does a growing keyhole mean?
back: A growing keyhole means the weld is about to burn through. The welder should speed up or lower the current.

front: What does a closing keyhole mean?
back: A closing keyhole means penetration is being lost. Incomplete joint penetration will follow unless the welder slows down or adds heat.

front: What are the 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G pipe positions?
back: 1G is rolled horizontal pipe. 2G is vertical pipe with a horizontal weld. 5G is fixed horizontal pipe. 6G is fixed pipe at 45°.

front: Why is the 5G pipe position difficult?
back: The pipe is fixed horizontal and cannot be turned. The welder works through flat, vertical and overhead positions in one weld.

front: What does a 6G pipe test qualify?
back: In common AWS structural practice, 6G qualifies all positions on pipe and plate groove welding, within the thickness and diameter range tested. Confirm against your code.

front: What does a 3G and 4G plate test qualify?
back: In common AWS structural practice, passing 3G and 4G on plate qualifies all positions of groove and fillet welding on plate. Confirm against your code.

front: Does a SMAW test qualify a welder for GMAW?
back: No. Changing the welding process requires a new test.

front: What is the E6010 electrode used for?
back: E6010 is a deep penetrating electrode run on direct current electrode positive. It is a standard choice for open root passes on pipe.

front: What is the E7018 electrode used for?
back: E7018 is a low hydrogen electrode used for fill and cap passes. It gives smooth, strong, ductile welds.

front: Why is E7018 stored in a heated rod oven?
back: Low hydrogen electrodes absorb moisture. Moisture puts hydrogen into the weld and can cause cracking, so oven temperature and time limits must be followed.

front: What does the 70 in E7018 mean?
back: It means the weld metal has a tensile strength of 70 ksi, or 70,000 pounds per square inch.

front: What does the T in E71T-1 mean?
back: T means tubular, so the wire is a flux cored wire. E71T-1 is a gas shielded wire that works in all positions.

front: What shielding gas is common for GMAW on steel?
back: A mix of 75 percent argon and 25 percent carbon dioxide is common. Always follow the WPS.

front: Which GMAW transfer mode suits out of position welding?
back: Short circuit transfer suits out of position welding and thin metal because it runs at low heat. Spray transfer works only in flat and horizontal.

front: What is the difference between gas shielded and self shielded FCAW?
back: Gas shielded flux cored wire needs outside shielding gas. Self shielded wire makes its own shielding from the flux in the core.

front: What shielding gas does GTAW use?
back: GTAW uses argon. The tungsten electrode does not melt and the filler rod is added by hand.

front: What is a purge in pipe welding?
back: A purge is argon fed inside the pipe so the back of the root weld sits in inert gas. It is used on metals such as stainless steel.

front: What is sugaring?
back: Sugaring is a gray, crusty oxidized surface on the back of a root weld caused by a poor purge.

front: What is a guided bend test?
back: A strip cut from the weld is bent into a U shape around a plunger. The convex outer surface is then checked for open discontinuities.

front: What is the difference between a face bend, root bend and side bend?
back: A face bend puts the weld face on the outside of the curve and a root bend puts the root there. A side bend stretches the full weld thickness and is used on thicker material.

front: What plunger diameter is common for a 3/8 inch bend specimen?
back: A common rule is 4 times the thickness, so 4 × 3/8 = 1.5 inches. Confirm in the code.

front: What is a common bend test limit on a single discontinuity?
back: In common AWS structural practice, no single discontinuity on the convex surface may exceed 1/8 inch in any direction. Confirm in your code.

front: What is a common limit on the sum of discontinuities in a bend test?
back: In common AWS structural practice, the sum of discontinuities over 1/32 inch and up to 1/8 inch may not exceed 3/8 inch. Confirm in your code.

front: How is heat input calculated?
back: Heat input in kJ per inch equals volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in inches per minute × 1,000). At 22 V, 100 A and 8 in/min it is 16.5 kJ/in.

front: What is the SENSE Level 2 module structure?
back: Level 2 has five compulsory modules plus optional plate, pipe and fabrication modules. The knowledge exam pass mark is 75 percent, except Level 1 safety which needs 100 percent.
